agree.reason: Because the memo admits the renovation helped and then argues for staff readiness and retention, a GM who credits the renovation is more likely to accept its people argument. It never makes a direct case against an outside candidate with experience at a larger hotel, though, so he may still lean that way.

honest.reason: The memo doesn't claim the writer was the main reason scores rose, and its figures come from the brief. Two claims go a little past the facts: "payroll savings already in place" has no dollar figure behind it, and "covered all of her responsibilities" sits awkwardly beside the admission that the writer has never handled the budget.

works_the_facts.reason: It turns the brief's numbers into useful figures: turnover of 64% vs 36%, training that is nearly twice as fast, and 81 vs 25 paid training shifts. It could have gone further by stating the 56 shifts saved outright, or by connecting the timing of the turnover drop to the 18-month score window.

right_comparison.reason: The before-and-after comparisons for turnover and training are accurate, but the memo never sets the writer against the real alternative, an outside hire. It only hints at that contrast with "I know the team, the building and our guests."

qualification.reason: The budget plan includes dates the GM can check: a review within 30 days, monthly variance meetings for six months, and a written plan to correct any overspend by the following month. It doesn't set a variance threshold or say what happens if the correction plan fails.

objections.reason: The memo deals head-on with the renovation objection and the lack of budget experience. It only answers the outside candidate's larger-hotel experience indirectly, through the seven weeks covering the role and the writer's six years at the hotel.

fit.reason: It's a written memo of about one page, delivered as the brief asked. It rightly declines to make the unsupported "main reason" claim the writer wanted.
